William Gurnall
WIL-yuhm GUR-nuhl
proper noun (person)
English Puritan pastor (1616-1679), vicar of Lavenham in Suffolk, author of The Christian in Complete Armour.

📖 Biblical Definition

William Gurnall was an English Puritan minister, vicar of Lavenham in Suffolk, remembered above all for one massive and enduring work: The Christian in Complete Armour, a vast practical exposition of the Christian's spiritual warfare from Ephesians 6:10-20. For more than a thousand pages Gurnall unfolds the whole armor of God piece by piece — the girdle of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit — pressing each upon the conscience with searching application and vivid imagery. Spurgeon said the book was "peerless and priceless," and that every line was full of wisdom. Gurnall's theme is that the Christian life is unrelenting combat against sin, Satan, and the world, and that the believer must be armed wholly in Christ, for partial armor is no armor at all. He conformed at the Restoration and kept his living, which brought him criticism from some nonconformists, yet his book has fed warring saints of every party ever since. Gurnall stands in the dictionary as the great Puritan anatomist of spiritual warfare, who taught the church that grace does not exempt the believer from battle but equips him for it.

WILLIAM GURNALL, proper noun. English Puritan minister (1616-1679), vicar of Lavenham, Suffolk.

Author of The Christian in Complete Armour, on the whole armor of God (Eph 6:10-20).

A vast, practical anatomy of the believer's warfare against sin, Satan, and the world.

Praised by Spurgeon as "peerless and priceless."

Taught that grace arms the Christian for battle rather than exempting him from it.

📖 Key Scripture

Eph 6:11 — "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil."

Eph 6:12 — "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Eph 6:13 — "Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand."

2 Cor 10:4 — "(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Gurnall's legacy is corrupted when the Puritans are caricatured as joyless legalists, and when the New Testament's call to spiritual warfare is softened into a comfortable religion with no enemy and no battle.

expand to see more

Killjoy-caricature correction. The popular slander paints the Puritans as dour, repressive, and joyless. Gurnall's life and book refute it: here is a pastor of vivid imagination, warm pastoral tenderness, and bracing hope, who armed weary saints for the fight with a thousand pages of comfort and counsel. The dictionary holds that the Puritan vision of the Christian life — serious, joyful, and full-blooded — is a treasure to recover, not a stereotype to repeat.

Warfare-denied misreading. Modern religion often empties the faith of conflict, offering self-improvement without an enemy. Gurnall recalls the church to the New Testament's sober realism: we wrestle against principalities and powers, and the believer who is not armed is already losing. The dictionary recovers the doctrine of spiritual warfare — the world, the flesh, and the devil are real foes, and the whole armor of God, which is Christ Himself, is the only sufficient defense.
